Financial Transaction Fraud Detection EDA¶

This notebook explores the PaySim financial transaction dataset for the V1 fraud detection project.

The goal of this notebook is to understand the data before building machine learning models. We will inspect the dataset structure, missing values, duplicate rows, class imbalance, transaction types, fraud patterns, and balance-related variables.

Important: This notebook does not train any model. Model training will be handled in the next notebook, 02_financial_ml_baseline.ipynb.

1. Import Libraries¶

We use only pandas for data analysis and matplotlib for visualization in this notebook.

In [71]:
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

pd.set_option("display.max_columns", None)
pd.set_option("display.float_format", "{:.4f}".format)

plt.style.use("default")

2. Load Dataset¶

The PaySim dataset should be placed manually at data/raw/financial/paysim.csv.

Because PaySim can be large, the code below first tries to load the full dataset. If a memory error occurs, it loads a smaller sample and clearly marks that the notebook is using sampled data.

In [72]:

6. Duplicate Row Check¶

Duplicate rows may indicate repeated records. We count duplicates before deciding whether any cleaning is required.

In [78]:

duplicate_percent = duplicate_count / len(df) * 100

print(f"Duplicate rows: {duplicate_count:,}")
print(f"Duplicate percentage: {duplicate_percent:.4f}%")

Duplicate rows: 0
Duplicate percentage: 0.0000%

Observation: Duplicate records should be reviewed carefully. If duplicates are true repeated transactions, they may need to be removed. If they represent valid repeated behavior, they may need to stay.

7. Fraud Class Distribution¶

The target column is isFraud. Fraud detection datasets are usually highly imbalanced, meaning fraudulent transactions are much rarer than normal transactions.

In [79]:
fraud_counts = df["isFraud"].value_counts().sort_index()
fraud_percent = df["isFraud"].value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index() * 100

fraud_distribution = pd.DataFrame({
    "count": fraud_counts,
    "percent": fraud_percent
})

fraud_distribution

isFraud

In [80]:
ax = fraud_counts.plot(kind="bar", color=["#4C78A8", "#E45756"], logy=True)
plt.title("Fraud Class Distribution (Log Scale)")
plt.xlabel("isFraud")
plt.ylabel("Number of Transactions (log scale)")
plt.xticks(rotation=0)

for index, value in enumerate(fraud_counts):
    ax.text(index, value, f"{value:,}", ha="center", va="bottom")

plt.show()
In [81]:
ax = fraud_percent.plot(kind="bar", color=["#4C78A8", "#E45756"])
plt.title("Fraud Class Distribution (%)")
plt.xlabel("isFraud")
plt.ylabel("Percentage of Transactions")
plt.xticks(rotation=0)

for index, value in enumerate(fraud_percent):
    ax.text(index, value, f"{value:.4f}%", ha="center", va="bottom")

plt.show()

Observation: This project is expected to have strong class imbalance. A normal bar chart can make the fraud class almost invisible, so the log-scale chart makes the minority class easier to see while still showing the large gap between normal and fraud transactions. The percentage chart makes the imbalance even clearer. Accuracy alone is not enough because a model could predict most transactions as normal and still achieve high accuracy while missing fraud cases. Metrics such as recall, precision, F1 score, ROC-AUC, and PR-AUC will be more useful.

9. Fraud Rate by Transaction Type¶

Fraud rate shows the percentage of transactions that are fraudulent within each transaction type.

In [84]:

fraud_rate_by_type = fraud_rate_by_type.rename(columns={
    "count": "total_transactions",
    "sum": "fraud_transactions",
    "mean": "fraud_rate"
})
fraud_rate_by_type["fraud_rate_percent"] = fraud_rate_by_type["fraud_rate"] * 100

Observation: Fraud rate is useful for imbalanced data because total transaction counts can hide risk. A transaction type may have many transactions but a low fraud rate, while another type may have fewer transactions but a much higher share of fraud. In PaySim, fraud is commonly associated with TRANSFER and CASH_OUT transactions.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))
axes = axes.flatten()

for ax, column in zip(axes, balance_columns):
    cap = df[column].quantile(0.99)
    normal_values = df.loc[df["isFraud"] == 0, column].clip(upper=cap)
    fraud_values = df.loc[df["isFraud"] == 1, column].clip(upper=cap)
    
    ax.hist(normal_values, bins=50, alpha=0.6, label="Normal", color="#4C78A8")
    ax.hist(fraud_values, bins=50, alpha=0.6, label="Fraud", color="#E45756")
    ax.set_title(column)
    ax.set_xlabel("Value capped at 99th percentile")
    ax.set_ylabel("Count")
    ax.legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observation: Balance fields may contain useful fraud signals. For feature engineering, we can create new variables such as origin balance change, destination balance change, and whether balances match the transaction amount.

13. Simple EDA Observations¶

Based on the analysis above:

  1. Class imbalance: Fraud transactions are much rarer than normal transactions. This means the model must be evaluated with fraud-focused metrics, not only accuracy.
  2. Important transaction types: Fraud is expected to be most associated with TRANSFER and CASH_OUT transactions in PaySim. Transaction type should be an important feature.
  3. Accuracy is not enough: If only a tiny percentage of transactions are fraud, a model can get high accuracy by predicting almost everything as normal. For fraud detection, missing fraud cases is costly, so recall, precision, F1 score, ROC-AUC, and PR-AUC are more meaningful.
  4. Balance features matter: Origin and destination balance changes may reveal suspicious transaction behavior and should be used for feature engineering.

14. Feature Relationship Exploration for Feature Engineering¶

This section creates temporary engineered features inside the notebook. These features are not saved to disk yet. The goal is to understand whether they may be useful for the next ML baseline notebook and later implementation in src/preprocessing.py.

In [93]:
eda_features = df.copy()

eda_features["orig_balance_change"] = eda_features["oldbalanceOrg"] - eda_features["newbalanceOrig"]
eda_features["dest_balance_change"] = eda_features["newbalanceDest"] - eda_features["oldbalanceDest"]
eda_features["orig_balance_error"] = eda_features["oldbalanceOrg"] - eda_features["newbalanceOrig"] - eda_features["amount"]
eda_features["dest_balance_error"] = eda_features["newbalanceDest"] - eda_features["oldbalanceDest"] - eda_features["amount"]
eda_features["amount_to_oldbalanceOrg_ratio"] = eda_features["amount"] / (eda_features["oldbalanceOrg"] + 1)
eda_features["is_orig_balance_drained"] = (eda_features["newbalanceOrig"] == 0).astype(int)
eda_features["is_high_risk_type"] = eda_features["type"].isin(["TRANSFER", "CASH_OUT"]).astype(int)

engineered_features = [
    "orig_balance_change",
    "dest_balance_change",
    "orig_balance_error",
    "dest_balance_error",
    "amount_to_oldbalanceOrg_ratio",
    "is_orig_balance_drained",
    "is_high_risk_type",
]

eda_features[engineered_features].head()

Correlation Matrix for Numeric and Engineered Features¶

A correlation matrix gives a quick view of relationships between numeric variables, engineered features, and the fraud label. Correlation does not prove causation, but it can help identify useful or redundant features.

Observation: Features with stronger relationships to isFraud are useful candidates for the ML baseline notebook. Features that are highly correlated with each other may carry overlapping information, so they should be monitored during model evaluation. For V1 preprocessing, the most useful candidates are likely orig_balance_change, dest_balance_change, orig_balance_error, dest_balance_error, amount_to_oldbalanceOrg_ratio, is_orig_balance_drained, and is_high_risk_type because they translate raw transaction fields into direct behavioral signals.

15. Fraud Rate Analysis for Representative Engineered Features¶

This section checks whether selected engineered features show fraud-related patterns. Instead of using these tables as model inputs, we use them to support the business logic behind feature engineering.

The five representative features are:

  • orig_balance_change: fund outflow from the origin account.
  • orig_balance_error: whether the origin balance change matches the transaction amount.
  • amount_to_oldbalanceOrg_ratio: transaction size relative to the origin account's starting balance.
  • is_orig_balance_drained: whether the origin account balance becomes zero after the transaction.
  • is_high_risk_type: whether the transaction is TRANSFER or CASH_OUT.

Binary Feature Fraud Rates¶

For binary features, we group transactions by feature value and calculate total transactions, fraud transactions, fraud rate, and fraud rate percentage.

In [99]:
binary_features = ["is_orig_balance_drained", "is_high_risk_type"]

binary_fraud_rate_tables = {}

for feature in binary_features:
    fraud_rate_table = eda_features.groupby(feature).agg(
        total_count=("isFraud", "count"),
        fraud_count=("isFraud", "sum"),
        fraud_rate=("isFraud", "mean")
    )
    fraud_rate_table["fraud_rate_percent"] = fraud_rate_table["fraud_rate"] * 100
    binary_fraud_rate_tables[feature] = fraud_rate_table

Observation: These binary fraud-rate tables show whether fraud is more common when a behavior is present. If the fraud rate is higher when is_orig_balance_drained = 1, account-draining behavior is a useful signal. If the fraud rate is higher when is_high_risk_type = 1, transaction type risk should be included in preprocessing.

Continuous Feature Fraud Rates by Quantile Bin¶

For continuous features, we create ten quantile bins using pd.qcut. Quantile bins help compare fraud rates across low, medium, and high ranges of a feature while keeping the number of transactions in each bin more balanced.

In [102]:
continuous_features = [
    "orig_balance_change",
    "orig_balance_error",
    "amount_to_oldbalanceOrg_ratio",
]

def calculate_quantile_fraud_rate(data, feature, q=10):
    temp = data[[feature, "isFraud"]].copy()
    bin_column = f"{feature}_bin"
    temp[bin_column] = pd.qcut(temp[feature], q=q, duplicates="drop")
    
    fraud_rate_table = temp.groupby(bin_column, observed=True).agg(
        total_count=("isFraud", "count"),
        fraud_count=("isFraud", "sum"),
        fraud_rate=("isFraud", "mean")
    )
    fraud_rate_table["fraud_rate_percent"] = fraud_rate_table["fraud_rate"] * 100
    return fraud_rate_table

continuous_fraud_rate_tables = {}

for feature in continuous_features:
    continuous_fraud_rate_tables[feature] = calculate_quantile_fraud_rate(eda_features, feature)

continuous_fraud_rate_tables["orig_balance_change"]

for feature in continuous_features:
    plot_data = continuous_fraud_rate_tables[feature]["fraud_rate_percent"]
    ax = plot_data.plot(kind="bar", figsize=(9, 4), color="#F58518")
    plt.title(f"Fraud Rate (%) by {feature} Quantile Bin")

    plt.ylabel("Fraud Rate (%)")
    plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha="right")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Observation: Fraud-rate analysis is useful in EDA because it connects raw transaction behavior with the target variable in a simple, interpretable way. If fraud rate changes across feature groups or bins, the feature is a stronger candidate for ML preprocessing. Based on this analysis, orig_balance_change, orig_balance_error, amount_to_oldbalanceOrg_ratio, is_orig_balance_drained, and is_high_risk_type should be considered for preprocessing.py.

Target leakage warning: These fraud-rate tables should not be directly used as training features. They are calculated using the target column isFraud, so turning the table values into model inputs would leak label information into training. The safe approach is to create the engineered features from transaction fields only, then let models learn patterns from the training data.

16. Final Summary¶

Dataset Overview¶

  • PaySim contains millions of financial transactions for simulated mobile money activity.
  • The target variable is isFraud, and it is highly imbalanced because fraud transactions are rare.

Fraud Pattern Findings¶

  • Fraud cases are concentrated in TRANSFER and CASH_OUT transaction types.
  • Fraud transactions show different amount and balance-change patterns from normal transactions.
  • Log-scale and percentage-based charts are useful because normal transactions heavily outnumber fraud transactions.

Feature Engineering Justification¶

  • The EDA supports creating behavior-based features from raw transaction fields.
  • orig_balance_change captures fund outflow from the origin account.
  • orig_balance_error captures origin-side balance consistency.
  • amount_to_oldbalanceOrg_ratio captures transaction size relative to origin balance.
  • is_orig_balance_drained captures account-draining behavior.
  • is_high_risk_type captures transaction-type risk for TRANSFER and CASH_OUT.
  • Destination-side features such as dest_balance_change and dest_balance_error may also be kept as supplementary fund-flow features in preprocessing.py, even though the main EDA justification focuses on the five representative features.

Evaluation Implication¶

  • Because fraud is rare, accuracy alone is not enough.
  • Later models should be evaluated using Recall, Precision, F1-score, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, and a confusion matrix.

Next Step¶

  • Build preprocessing.py to create these engineered features consistently.
  • Use 02_financial_ml_baseline.ipynb to compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost.
  • Select one primary supervised fraud detection model for the V1 risk scoring system.
